runs.s: Most holy name for God in the OT, usually translated “Lord.”
One of the fortified cities of Naphtali’s tribe (Joshua 19:38). Some have identified Yiron with the present village of Jarun, southeast of Bint Jebeil.

The wooden bar that allowed two (or more) draft animals to be coupled (yoked) so that they might effectively work together (Numbers 19:2; 1 Kgs 19:19; Job 1:3). In addition to this literal usage, the Bible frequently uses the term metaphorically to refer to work or bondage (Leviticus 26:13). The yoke of bondage was applied not only by foreign oppressors but often by Israel’s own kings as well (1 Kgs 12:4-14; 2 Chr 10:4-14). In prophetic writings, the yoke of bondage was generally associated with divine judgment (Lamentations 1:14), so that deliverance was represented as God breaking the yoke that had enslaved Israel (Isaiah 9:4; Isaiah 10:27; Isaiah 14:25; Isaiah 58:6; Jeremiah 2:20; Jeremiah 5:5). The yoke of bondage figured prominently in Jeremiah’s dispute with Hananiah’s prophecy concerning Judah’s imminent release from Babylonian captivity (Jeremiah 27:8-11; Jeremiah 28:1-17). In the NT, Jesus transforms “yoke” into a positive term by calling on people to take up his yoke, which is not burdensome, and he will give them rest for their souls (Matthew 11:29-30).
One of the feast days of Israel involving atonement for the sins of the nation (Leviticus 23:26-32).
